subject: John the Baptist
note: Evidence for John the Baptist's figure page. Every quotation is in john-the-baptist.quotes.json and passes verify-quotes.mjs. Fetched texts are in design/saints-hub/sources/people/john-the-baptist/ (gitignored). Bible lines are the Berean Standard Bible (public domain): the verses used are copied into bsb-john-the-baptist-verses.txt; Luke 1 is read from shared/bsb-berean-standard-bible.txt. The Catena Aurea on Matthew 11 (Newman's 1841 translation) was copied from sources/oak-sources/gregory/, where the personality test's research fetched it.

life.text: Zechariah was a priest of the division of Abijah; Elizabeth was a descendant of Aaron; both were old and childless. Gabriel announced John's birth to Zechariah at the altar of incense; Zechariah doubted and was struck silent.
Elizabeth was in her sixth month at the Annunciation; Luke calls her Mary's relative (not cousin); the baby leaped at Mary's greeting; Mary stayed about three months.
life.source: Luke 1:26, 36, 39-45, 56 (BSB). The Catholic Encyclopedia renders the word "cousin" (syggenis); the BSB has "relative" and Luke gives no degree of kinship.

life.text: Named John on the eighth day; Zechariah wrote "His name is John" and spoke again; the Benedictus; the child lived in the wilderness until his public appearance.
life.source: Luke 1:57-80 (BSB). Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, 24 June: "Zechariah uttered a canticle of praise, the Benedictus".

life.text: Birthplace: Luke names only "a town in the hill country of Judah". Britannica: born "Judaea, Palestine, near Jerusalem"; "localized at ʿEn Kerem from at least 530 ce".
Dates: Britannica gives "died 28–36 ce"; public ministry prominent "In 27/28 or 28/29"; Aretas's victory over Herod in 35–36 came after John's execution.
The word of God came to him in the fifteenth year of Tiberius; camel's hair, leather belt, locusts and wild honey; crowds from Jerusalem and Judea; baptised in the Jordan; never took wine.
His preaching to crowds, tax collectors and soldiers; people wondered if he was the Christ.
Places he baptised: Bethany beyond the Jordan, Aenon near Salim.
He baptised Jesus; tried to prevent Him; saw the Spirit descend like a dove.
Priests and Levites asked who he was: not the Christ, not Elijah, not the Prophet; "a voice".
"Look, the Lamb of God"; two disciples followed Jesus; one was Andrew, who found Simon.
"He must increase; I must decrease", when his disciples reported everyone going to Jesus.
His disciples fasted often and he taught them to pray.
Imprisoned for rebuking Herod's marriage to Herodias; Herod feared him and listened gladly.
The question from prison, sent by two disciples; Jesus' answer and His praise of John.
Hilary, Jerome and Chrysostom each say John asked for his disciples' sake, not his own.
life.source: Catena Aurea on Matthew 11 (tr. 1841): Hilary, "John then is providing not for his own, but his disciples' ignorance"; Jerome, "Therefore he does not ask as being himself ignorant"; Chrysostom, "when he was going to die, he was more concerned on their behalf".
life.note: Jerome's comment in the Catena also gives an earlier reading of his own (John asks whether to announce Christ in the world below), which Chrysostom rejects; the page gives only what all three agree on.

life.text: "John never performed a sign".
About twelve disciples at Ephesus knew only John's baptism; Apollos too.
Titles: "surnamed 'the Baptist' (i.e. Baptizer) even during his lifetime"; "the Precursor"; the Orthodox "Forerunner".
life.source: Catholic Encyclopedia, "St. John the Baptist"; Roman Martyrology 1916 ("precursor of our Lord"); OCA, 7 January.

life.text: Patron of baptism, monastics, hermits, converts, tailors, prisoners "and many other occupations and causes".

death.text: The banquet, the dance, the oath, the request prompted by Herodias, the beheading in prison; the disciples buried the body and told Jesus; Jesus withdrew; Herod later thought Jesus was John risen.

Josephus: Herod feared John's influence might lead to rebellion; John was sent a prisoner to Machaerus and put to death there; some Jews saw the destruction of Herod's army by Aretas as God's punishment. Machaerus lay "in the borders of the dominions of Aretas and Herod"; Aretas is "The King Of Arabia" in the chapter heading.
death.source: Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.1-2, tr. Whiston (Gutenberg #2848). Eusebius, Church History 1.11, quotes the same passage.

death.text: Josephus names Herodias's daughter Salome, married to Philip the tetrarch; he does not tell of the dance. Herod Antipas and Herod (Philip) were sons of Herod the Great.
death.source: Josephus, Antiquities 18.5.4, tr. Whiston: "Herodias ... was married to Herod [Philip], the son of Herod the Great ... who had a daughter, Salome ... was married to Herod [Antipas], her husband's brother by the father's side ... her daughter Salome was married to Philip, the son of Herod, and tetrarch of Trachonitis".

death.text: Tomb at Sebaste attested from 360; Theodoret says under Julian his coffin was opened, bones burnt, ashes scattered.
death.source: Britannica ("The traditional burial site, at Sebaste ... is attested from 360 onward"); Theodoret, Church History 3.3 (NPNF2 3). The Catholic Encyclopedia gives the same, from Rufinus and Theodoret, dated c. 362.

death.text: The head: OCA tells three findings (Mount of Olives; near Emesa in 452; a third about 850); the Coptic synaxarium, 2 Tout: "It is also said that the head now is present at Homs in Syria"; the 1916 Martyrology, 29 August: carried to Rome, kept in St Silvester near Campo Marzio; the Catholic Encyclopedia lists Amiens, Nemours, St-Jean d'Angély and S. Silvestro in Capite as claimants and says the accounts are "so intricate as to baffle solution".
death.source: OCA 24 February and 25 May; CopticChurch.net, Tout 2; Roman Martyrology (1916), 29 August; Catholic Encyclopedia.
death.note: The Umayyad Mosque's shrine in Damascus is a well-known claim, but no fetched source states it, so the page leaves it out. The OCA's later traditions (the head speaking after death, Herodias piercing the tongue, Salome's death on the ice) are not on the page.

myths.text: Carob: Britannica: "The names locust bean and St. John's bread stem from the belief that the 'locusts' on which John the Baptist fed were carob pods." Leviticus 11:22 allows eating locusts.
Seven veils: the stage direction "Salomé dances the dance of the seven veils." Robert Ross's note in the same edition: "Written in French in 1892".
myths.source: Oscar Wilde, Salomé, tr. Alfred Douglas (1894), Project Gutenberg #42704.
myths.note: Other sources date the writing to late 1891; the page follows the edition it quotes.

myths.text: Baptists: "Most scholars agree that Baptists originated within 17th-century Puritanism"; they hold that only believers should be baptized, by immersion.
Two Herods: Herod (the Great) died while Jesus was a child (Matthew 2:19-22); John was killed by "Herod the tetrarch" (Matthew 14:1), the Herod to whom Pilate sent Jesus (Luke 23:6-12).

elijah.text: Malachi 4:5; Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14; 17:10-13; John 1:21; 2 Kings 1:8 with Matthew 3:4 (the leather belt).

Jerome: John is called Elias not by metempsychosis but because he came in the spirit and power of Elias; the parallel of Ahab and Jezebel with Herod and Herodias. Chrysostom: "John the Baptist is Elias, and Elias is John, because both were forerunners of Christ", after joining Malachi 4:5 and Malachi 3:1.
elijah.note: The Catena labels the source only "Jerome"; the page calls it his Commentary on Matthew, which is where the Catena's Jerome on Matthew comes from.

tidbits.text: Solmization: Guido of Arezzo, an 11th-century Italian monk, took ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la from the Latin hymn "Ut queant laxis", whose first six lines begin on successively higher notes; ut was later replaced by do. The Catholic Encyclopedia names "Ut queant laxis" as the hymn of Paul the Deacon "composed in honour of the saint".
Augustine: "Christ was born when the days were just beginning to lengthen; John was born when they began to shorten."
OCA, 29 August: "also a strict fast day ... In some Orthodox cultures pious people will not eat food from a flat plate, use a knife, or eat food that is round in shape on this day."
tidbits.source: OCA, The Beheading of John the Baptist.

tidbits.text: Only Mary's and John's births (with Christ's) are kept: the 1916 Martyrology's note says "birthday" means the day a saint enters heaven, "However, the Blessed Virgin and St. John the Baptist are exceptions to this rule." The Catholic Encyclopedia asks why his feast is his nativity, "whereas with other saints it is the day of their death".
tidbits.source: Roman Martyrology (1916), introductory note; Catholic Encyclopedia.
tidbits.note: Used in "Is he a saint?" (big line). A tidbit on the Battle of Fontenay (841, Catholic Encyclopedia) was written and then cut to fit the numbers column.

feasts.text: 24 June: Nativity, Catholic solemnity (USCCB 2026; Calendarium Romanum 1969 "In Nativitate S. Ioannis Baptistae, Sollemnitas"); Church of England Festival ("The Birth of John the Baptist" in the list of Festivals); Episcopal (LFF 2022); LCMS (LSB calendar; the text extraction shows the day number as 25, beside the Augsburg Confession's 25: an extraction slip, the LSB keeps 24 June); ELCA ("24 JOHN THE BAPTIST").
feasts.source: usccb-2026cal.txt, calendarium-romanum-1969-ocr.txt, cofe-calendar.txt, lff2022.txt, lsb-calendar.txt, elca-churchyear.txt (shared).

feasts.text: 29 August: "The Passion of Saint John the Baptist", Memorial (USCCB 2026; Calendarium "Memoria"); Church of England "The Beheading of John the Baptist"; Episcopal "The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist" (LFF 2022, page for 29 August); LCMS "The Martyrdom of St John the Baptist". No 29 August entry was found in the ELCA list, so the ELCA is not named for it.

OCA: Synaxis 7 January; First and Second Finding 24 February; Third Finding 25 May ("about the year 850"); Nativity 24 June; Beheading 29 August (strict fast); Conception 23 September. Six days in all.
feasts.source: OCA day pages and lives, fetched 2026-09-25.

feasts.text: Coptic: Paona 30, "The Nativity of St. John, the Baptist"; Tout 2, "The Martyrdom of St. John the Baptist". Tout 1 = 11 September (12 before a Gregorian leap year), so Tout 2 = 12 September (13); Paoni 30 = 7 July.
feasts.source: CopticChurch.net synaxarium; shared/wikipedia-coptic-calendar.txt for the correspondence.

feasts.text: Six months before Christmas (LFF 2022: "His birth is celebrated six months before Christmas Day, since, according to Luke, Elizabeth became pregnant six months before the angel Gabriel appeared to Mary"). Catholic Encyclopedia: the Nativity "is one of the oldest feasts, if not the oldest feast, introduced into both the Greek and Latin liturgies to honour a saint". 1916 Martyrology, 29 August: "put to death by Herod about the feast of Easter ... the solemn commemoration takes place today, when his venerable head was found for the second time".

kin.text: Chrysostom's sermon: "Again Herodias raves; again she is troubled; she dances again; and again desires to receive John's head in a charger."
Martin at Maximus's court: "in Martin alone, apostolic authority continued to assert itself."
kin.source: Sulpicius Severus, Life of St Martin 20 (NPNF2 11), shared/npnf211.txt.

pictures.text: Band: John the Baptist, detail of the Ghent Altarpiece (Deesis, front panel), Jan van Eyck, 1432, St Bavo's Cathedral, Ghent. Commons licence tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-auto-expired|deathyear=1441}}. 1700 x 2262 on Commons (a scan: the file page says "Scanned with HP PSC 2400"); smoothed with a 1 px blur to take out the print screen, resized to 1353 x 1800, light unsharp mask, JPEG quality 78: 387 KB. posM 45% 12%, posD 45% 20% (face at about 30% of the height, 45% across).
pictures.note: Other versions of the same panel on Commons: Hubert van Eyck 026.jpg (Yorck, 2024 x 2437, darker), WGA07634 (900 x 1195). Other candidates looked at: Titian (Accademia, full length, face small), Mengs (Houston), Andrea del Sarto (small files), Champaigne (small file). The personality test's face (Geertgen tot Sint Jans) and Doré's plate are not used.

pictures.text: Second picture: St John the Forerunner, Russian icon of the 19th century, Chester Beatty Library WX 40 (Google Arts & Culture). Commons licence tag {{PD-Art|PD-old-100-1923}}. 4980 x 5622; cropped to the central panel (19% to 81% of the width, 2% to 90% of the height), resized to 936 x 1500, quality 85: 249 KB. He points to the Christ Child (cross halo, IC XC) lying in a bowl; a small blessing figure in clouds above.
pictures.note: Caption's "angelos": Gregory the Great in the Catena on Matthew 11:10, "For the Greek word Angel, is in Latin Nuntius, 'a messenger.'"

could_not_verify: The Umayyad Mosque's claim to the head (Damascus): no fetched source; left out.

Gregory the Great's line "in spirit he was Elias, in person he was not" (Homily 7, on John 1:21): the Catena on John could not be fetched from CCEL (404); Jerome and Chrysostom from the Catena on Matthew 11 are used instead.
The OCA's date for John's death ("in the year 32"): not used; the page gives Britannica's 28 to 36.
The Greek churches' and the Russian Church's own calendars for his days: not fetched, so only the OCA and the 13-day rule are given.
Whether the ELCA keeps 29 August: not found in the ELW list, so not claimed.

checker_2026_09_25.by: One light checking pass (Moses, Gideon, John the Baptist), 2026-09-25
checked: Read on disk: Britannica, En Kerem 'from at least 530'; the Catholic Encyclopedia, the Nativity 'one of the oldest feasts, if not the oldest feast' to honour a saint, and the head 'so intricate as to baffle solution'.

Feasts read in the calendar texts: USCCB 24 June (solemnity) and 29 August 'The Passion of Saint John the Baptist'; Church of England 24 June and 29 August; LFF 2022 both days; LSB 24 June and 29 August; ELCA 24 June only; OCA six days (the second finding in 452, the third 'about the year 850'); 1916 Martyrology 29 August 'about the feast of Easter', 'found for the second time', St Silvester near Campo Marzio; Coptic 30 Paoni = 7 July and 2 Tout = 12 September.

Attributions: in the Catena on Matthew 11, Hilary, Jerome ('he does not ask as being himself ignorant') and Chrysostom all say he sent his disciples for their sake; Jerome and Chrysostom on Elijah; Josephus names Salome; Wilde's stage direction.
Disputes each in its own words: Was he Elijah? (four panels, no winner); where his head is (OCA, Coptic, Rome, Amiens, then the Catholic Encyclopedia).

Rules: capitals in our text and quotations; 'Saint' in the seo title is allowed for a New Testament saint; no section marks; licences read on Commons (PD-Art|PD-old-auto-expired; PD-Art|PD-old-100-1923); sizes match; Doré's john-the-baptist.jpg untouched.

changed: Circle, Mary: 'calling John and Jesus cousins is a guess' dismissed the tradition in our voice. Now: Luke never says how they were related, 'so John and Jesus were kin, but not certainly cousins.'

'Was he Elijah?' lede: 'The last lines of the Old Testament' is true only of the Protestant order (Catholic Bibles end the Old Testament with Maccabees). Now: 'The book of Malachi ends with a promise'.
for_owner: The writer's open questions stand: the soft 1700 px Ghent scan (387 KB), the winged icon, and that Elijah's page should agree with this page's 'Was he Elijah?' (link rather than repeat).
